title: Marketing Research Digest — Retail & E-Commerce — 2026-09-30 (Part 2)
journals_not_indexed: Journal of Consumer Satisfaction, Dissatisfaction and Complaining Behavior
Journal of Empirical Generalisations in Marketing Science
Marketing Science Institute Working Paper Series

studies.title: Pickup lockers don't cannibalize home delivery — they keep customers from leaving
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: The Double-Edged Offline Touchpoint: How Self-Pickup Stations Reshape Pure-Play E-Commerce Transactions
studies.the_study: Researchers used a synthetic difference-in-differences design on individual-level transaction data from an Asian pure-play e-commerce platform to measure what happens when the platform opens self-pickup stations near customers. Spending and shopping frequency rose, and home delivery orders were not cannibalized. The gain came almost entirely from reduced churn and deeper engagement among existing shoppers rather than from new customer acquisition — and the benefit shrank when stations were placed close to major offline retail alternatives.
studies.why_it_matters: Click-and-collect is usually justified as a logistics cost play; this suggests its real return is customer retention, and that the wrong location can hand your traffic to a competing physical store.
studies.story_angle_primary: Retention, not acquisition, may be the right KPI for click-and-collect rollouts — and location screening should explicitly penalize sites adjacent to strong offline rivals. Worth testing in your own network before assuming the Asian platform's geometry transfers.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For shoppers, a locker down the street quietly changes how often you order online — the convenience of pickup appears to make people stick with one platform rather than shop around.
studies.caveats: Single platform in a single Asian market; quasi-experimental rather than randomized; results may not generalize to markets with different store density or delivery economics.
studies.verdict_notes: Core findings match the abstract; two of the three named moderators (station accessibility, product attributes) are dropped.

studies.title: Putting EV chargers in the parking lot lifted German grocery revenue 3.4%
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: EV Charging Availability and Grocery Store Performance
studies.the_study: Using a staggered difference-in-differences design across more than 300 stores of a leading German grocery chain, researchers found that adding EV charging to store parking lots increased revenue by 3.4%. The lift came from more transactions rather than bigger baskets, peaked during off-peak weekend hours, and reflected market stealing from competitors as well as market expansion. Effects were stronger in stores and neighborhoods with particular characteristics, including surface-to-parking ratio, local competition, and the mix of apartments versus houses.
studies.why_it_matters: It quantifies a hard-to-value amenity investment and reframes chargers as a traffic-driving and competitive-defense tool, not just a sustainability gesture.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat charger installation as a store-network location problem: the data suggest rollout should be prioritized where parking is ample, competition is close, and shoppers live in apartments without home charging. Test whether off-peak weekend staffing and promotions can capture the incremental trips.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Charging your car takes 30 minutes you have to spend somewhere — and this shows how retailers turn that waiting time into extra shopping trips.
studies.caveats: One grocery chain in one country; quasi-experimental design; charger placement was not randomized, so site selection may partly drive results.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, sample and the 3.4% effect are reported accurately; the story angle assigns directions to store/market moderators that the abstract does not state.

studies.title: Not knowing what you want can make you more likely to buy
studies.paper_title: Turning Uncertainty into Opportunity: Preference Uncertainty Can Be Beneficial When Consumers Have Outcome Uncertainty
studies.the_study: Across a set of experiments, researchers separated two kinds of uncertainty: not knowing what you want (preference uncertainty) and not knowing what the product will deliver (outcome uncertainty). When outcome uncertainty is inherently high — think the flavor profile of a wine — consumers who were unsure of their own preferences reported higher purchase intent than those with clear preferences. The mechanism was optimism: with fuzzy preferences, many possible outcomes could turn out to be the perfect match, whereas a precise preference means only one can.
studies.why_it_matters: It inverts the standard assumption that marketers should always help consumers clarify what they want; in unpredictable categories, preference-clarifying tools may actually suppress purchase.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit whether your category has high inherent outcome variability (wine, craft beer, fragrance, specialty coffee, experiential travel). If so, test whether quizzes and preference-profiling tools help or hurt conversion — they may be closing off the optimism that drives the sale.
studies.story_angle_secondary: That pleasant feeling of browsing an unfamiliar wine list may be partly self-deception: when you're unsure what you like, your brain assumes more of the options could be great.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies measuring purchase intent rather than observed purchases; sample composition and size not specified in the abstract; effect is specific to categories where outcomes are genuinely unpredictable.
studies.verdict_notes: Uncertainty types, direction of effect, optimism mechanism and the purchase-intent outcome all match; caveats correctly note unspecified samples.

studies.title: Stop storing your keepsakes — using them makes them mean more
studies.paper_title: Growing sentimental value through object usage
studies.the_study: Across five studies, researchers tested what happens to a sentimentally valuable object when people actually use it versus store it away for protection. Using the object repeatedly increased its sentimental value, because each use makes the underlying association salient again, which leads people to feel the association is more deeply integrated into their self-concept — a cycle that further boosts the object's value.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives brands selling gifts, heirlooms, and commemorative products a reason to actively encourage use rather than preservation, and suggests the durability of a product's emotional hold depends on it staying in circulation.
studies.story_angle_primary: Gift, jewelry, and memorabilia brands could test messaging and packaging that nudges toward everyday use rather than display or storage — a used keepsake may generate more attachment, more repurchase, and more word of mouth than one in a drawer.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The china you never take out and the watch you keep in its box may be losing meaning, not gaining it — the research suggests handling sentimental objects is what keeps them special.
studies.caveats: Laboratory and online experiments rather than long-run field observation; sample details not given in the abstract; short time horizons relative to the multi-year nature of real sentimental attachment.
studies.verdict_notes: Five studies, direction of effect and the salience/self-concept mechanism match; the caveat asserts a study format the abstract never states.

studies.title: Virtual streamers sell fun; human streamers sell function
studies.paper_title: Human or Virtual? A Study on Consumer Preferences for E‐Commerce Streamers
studies.the_study: In two scenario-based experiments grounded in social presence theory, researchers tested how streamer type (human versus virtual avatar) interacts with product type (utilitarian versus hedonic) in live commerce. Human streamers produced higher purchase intent for utilitarian products, while virtual streamers did better for hedonic ones, with social presence mediating the effect and brand trust strengthening the link between social presence and purchase intent.
studies.why_it_matters: As brands weigh cheaper, always-on virtual hosts against human influencers, this suggests the choice should follow the product category rather than the cost line.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands experimenting with AI avatars in live shopping could A/B test host type by product category — the hypothesis worth checking is that avatars underperform on practical, high-consideration items where buyers want a real person vouching.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If a cartoon host is selling you makeup and a real person is selling you a vacuum, that may not be an accident — the format is being matched to how you make each kind of decision.
studies.caveats: Two hypothetical scenario experiments measuring stated purchase intent, not real purchases; sample size and country not specified in the abstract; single mechanism tested in a fast-changing format.
studies.verdict_notes: Two scenario-based experiments, the streamer-by-product interaction, social-presence mediation and brand-trust moderation are all reported as in the abstract; "high-consideration" in the story angle is an added descriptor but is framed as a hypothesis to test.

studies.title: The "imported goods" endcap that made imported goods sell 30% worse
studies.paper_title: Data-driven analysis of the impact of imported product displays in supermarkets on purchase behaviour and differences by country
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a 60-day field test with a local supermarket chain in Turkiye: eight imported snack items were pulled out of their normal category shelves and grouped onto a dedicated "imported products" endcap in one store, with a matched control store tracked for comparison. Unit sales of those items fell 30.28% versus the control. A follow-up online survey (189 respondents in Turkiye, 199 in England) found purchase intention was also lower in the dedicated-display scenario than in within-category shelf placement in both countries, with display format mattering more than country.
studies.why_it_matters: Special display fixtures are treated as a near-automatic sales lift in retail planning and are often paid for by suppliers, yet here isolating products from their category removed the comparison context shoppers apparently rely on and destroyed nearly a third of sales.
studies.story_angle_primary: Retailers and brand managers who buy or grant endcap and themed-display space should treat it as a hypothesis to be tested store-by-store, not a guaranteed uplift — especially for products whose appeal depends on being compared against domestic alternatives on the shelf. This is one chain and one category, so the practical move is to run matched-store A/B tests before committing display budgets.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers apparently decide about imported snacks by weighing them against the familiar options right next to them; move the import to its own special stand and it loses the reference point that justified the price. It's a reminder that where something sits in a store changes how good a deal it seems.
studies.caveats: Field test covers only two stores, one chain, one country and eight imported snack items; the second study is an online survey using hypothetical scenarios and stated purchase intention, explaining about 20% of variance. No pre-registration detail reported.
studies.verdict_notes: Sales decline, survey Ns, country comparison and variance explained all match; the field test window is described slightly inaccurately.

studies.title: When buyers and sellers get too friendly, the platform loses the transaction
studies.paper_title: Relationship network stability and fewer on-platform transactions: evidence from a freight marketplace
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.the_study: Using longitudinal transaction data from a leading Chinese freight exchange platform, researchers measured how stable each user's trading-partner network was across periods and modeled it against continued on-platform activity with two-way fixed effects. Carriers with more stable partner networks made fewer subsequent transactions on the platform; relationship dissolution was associated with fewer transactions, while forming new relationships was associated with more. The pattern did not hold robustly for shippers, suggesting the two sides of the marketplace behave differently.
studies.why_it_matters: Marketplaces spend heavily to create good matches, but the better the match sticks, the more the pair has reason to trade directly and bypass the platform — a structural tension for any intermediary that bills per transaction.
studies.story_angle_primary: Platform operators should look at whether their own "successful match" metric is quietly predicting churn, and consider governance and pricing that reward repeat relationships on-platform (subscriptions, escrow, insurance, financing) rather than only per-transaction search fees. Note the effect appeared on the supply side only, so the two market sides may need different retention designs.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It explains a familiar dynamic: once you've found a good plumber, driver or supplier through an app, you stop using the app. The relationship, not the platform, becomes the infrastructure.
studies.caveats: Single platform in a single country and industry (Chinese freight); associational fixed-effects evidence rather than an experiment, and the paper itself frames results as consistent with, not proof of, the disintermediation interpretation.
studies.verdict_notes: Data source, two-way fixed effects, direction of the carrier associations, the shipper non-robustness and the paper's own hedged interpretation are all represented correctly.

studies.title: Chatbots that get local culture make a foreign retailer feel like a hometown brand
studies.paper_title: When chatbots speak local: cultural understanding as a driver of value co-creation
studies.the_study: A mixed-methods study of a cross-border online retailer operating in one collectivist emerging market combined 15 semi-structured consumer interviews with a survey-based field study of 303 online consumers analyzed via structural equation modeling. Chatbots perceived as culturally fluent raised perceived brand localness, which fed consumer–brand identification and, in turn, value co-creation behaviors such as feedback and advocacy. Consumer ethnocentrism did not moderate the effect, suggesting even nationally-minded shoppers responded to culturally attuned bots.
studies.why_it_matters: As retailers deploy LLM-based service agents globally, this suggests the localization payoff goes beyond translation: cultural register in the chat window can shift how "foreign" the whole brand feels.
studies.story_angle_primary: International e-commerce teams could test culturally localized chatbot personas — idiom, humor, holidays, service etiquette — against literal translation and measure downstream identification and advocacy, not just resolution rate. The evidence comes from one retailer in one market and relies on self-reported responses, so treat it as a promising hypothesis for A/B testing rather than an established lift.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The chatbot that knows your local slang and holidays isn't an accident — it's a deliberate lever to make a distant company feel like it belongs where you live. Worth noticing the next time a support bot sounds unexpectedly familiar.
studies.caveats: Single cross-border retailer in one collectivist emerging market; survey-based self-report with cross-sectional structure limiting causal claims; qualitative phase N=15.
studies.verdict_notes: Mixed-methods design (15 interviews, 303 online-recruited consumers, SEM), the localness–identification–co-creation chain, the null ethnocentrism moderation and the single-retailer/single-market boundary all match the abstract.

studies.title: Chinese shoppers reward ESG only when they believe you mean it
studies.paper_title: Authentic or strategic ESG? Motive attribution, consumer–company identification and purchase intention in retailing
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: Two studies with Chinese retail consumers tested how ESG messaging converts into purchase intention: a cross-sectional survey (N=226) mapping the pathways, and a two-condition between-subjects experiment (N=156) manipulating whether corporate ESG actions were framed as sincerely motivated or strategically calculated. ESG performance raised purchase intention even among skeptical consumers, but the effect ran substantially through consumer–company identification, and only sincere-motive framing activated that identification — the identification pathway accounted for 38.3% of the total effect.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the return on ESG spending depends less on the disclosure itself than on whether shoppers read the motive as genuine, which is a communications problem as much as an operations one.
studies.story_angle_primary: Sustainability communicators can test framing that foregrounds values, history and costs borne rather than awards and metrics, and measure whether it moves identification — the mediating variable that carried most of the effect here. The experiment is small and scenario-based, so treat it as direction for message testing rather than proof.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Consumers are running a motive check on every green claim: the same recycled packaging reads as principle or as PR depending on how it's explained, and that judgment predicts whether they buy.
studies.caveats: Single country (China); small experimental sample (N=156 across two conditions, under 100 per cell); survey study is cross-sectional and cannot establish causation; outcome is stated purchase intention, not observed purchases.
studies.verdict_notes: Study designs, Ns and the 38.3% indirect effect are correct, but one story-angle line overstates the identification channel as carrying most of the effect.

studies.title: Hand sanitizer stations still earn their keep: visible hygiene cues soften shoppers' dislike of crowded stores
studies.paper_title: Shared but feared: A vulnerability-sensitive account of consumer responses to post-crisis service environments
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a two-part study inside a single French-language survey (N=425) of post-pandemic consumers. Part one found that lingering fear of infection raised health anxiety, but only self-focused personal health anxiety predicted avoiding public service settings. Part two experimentally varied store density (high vs. low) and the presence of sanitary signals: crowding lowered shopping satisfaction, but that penalty shrank when visible hygiene cues were present, and the benefit of those cues was largest among shoppers who remained most worried about infection.
studies.why_it_matters: Many retailers have quietly stripped out the pandemic-era hygiene signage and sanitizer stations; this suggests those cues still function as a cheap buffer against the satisfaction hit that comes with busy stores.
studies.story_angle_primary: Worth testing rather than assuming: run a split test keeping visible sanitary cues in a subset of high-traffic stores and track satisfaction and dwell time at peak hours. The study also suggests segmentation value, since the shoppers who respond most are those still carrying residual health anxiety.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For consumers, the finding puts a name to a vague feeling: a packed store bothers people less when there are visible signs someone is managing the risk. It also shows post-pandemic wariness is mostly about protecting yourself, not about others.
studies.caveats: Single country (French-language sample), one survey pool used for both studies, an experimental manipulation of store scenarios rather than observed behavior in real stores, and satisfaction measured as stated response; the moderation by residual fear was exploratory.
studies.verdict_notes: N, two-study structure inside one survey, and the density-by-sanitary-signal result are right; the digest conflates manipulated density with perceived crowding and omits the null mediation, and it asserts a single country not stated in the abstract.

studies.title: The borderless freelance marketplace isn't: four frictions that quietly kill creative work on global platforms
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: Cross-Border Tensions in Creative Service Delivery on Global Professional Digital Platforms
studies.the_study: Using a sequential mixed-methods design, researchers conducted 40 semi-structured interviews with freelancers, clients and platform stakeholders across 17 countries, then analyzed 27,427 unsolicited online community discussions. They identified four recurring tensions — organizing, performing, belonging and learning — that systematically constrain freelancers' creative work, sharpened by culturally divergent service norms and Global North–South economic asymmetries.
studies.why_it_matters: Brands increasingly buy creative work through platforms like these; the study maps where the platform's own architecture, not the talent, degrades the output.
studies.story_angle_primary: For brand and agency leaders sourcing creative work offshore: audit your briefing, revision and rating practices against these four tensions, since platform metrics that reward speed and compliance can suppress the creative risk-taking you are paying for.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A window into the reality behind the gig-economy promise — the same rating systems and 24-hour responsiveness norms that make platforms convenient for buyers create structural disadvantages for workers in lower-income countries.
studies.caveats: Qualitative and discourse-based evidence, so no causal test of how these tensions affect work quality or earnings; interview sample is modest and self-selected, and community discourse skews toward people motivated to post about problems.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, samples and the four tensions match the abstract; headline verb and one story-angle specific go slightly beyond it.

studies.title: Blended burgers keep surprising people: review of 79 studies finds hybrid meat wins on taste more often than expected
studies.paper_title: Consumers’ psychological constructs regarding hybrid meat products: a scoping review
studies.the_study: A scoping review synthesized 79 peer-reviewed publications published through December 2025 on consumer psychology around hybrid meat products — items blending animal protein with plant or alternative protein — across retail, restaurant and experimental settings. Acceptance, liking and preference were generally high and frequently exceeded consumers' own expectations, sensory appeal was the strongest predictor of liking, and non-meat ratios ranging from 1% all the way to 80% were broadly accepted. Messaging mattered too: environmental and health framings had the greatest positive effect on adoption.
studies.why_it_matters: For grocers and food brands, hybrids look like a lower-resistance path to reducing meat content than full plant-based substitutes — and the evidence suggests the ceiling on how much meat you can replace is higher than most product teams assume.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test reformulation ratios more aggressively than intuition suggests, and pair the product with environmental or health messaging rather than hiding the blend; the sensory bar, not the concept, is what determines acceptance.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Consumers who reject meat substitutes outright often like hybrid products when they actually taste them — a reminder that expectations about plant protein tend to be worse than the reality on the plate.
studies.caveats: This is a narrative scoping review, not a meta-analysis, so no pooled effect sizes; the underlying studies are heterogeneous, many use single-session taste tests rather than repeat purchasing, and long-term behavioral adaptation is explicitly flagged as unstudied.
studies.verdict_notes: Review scope, 79 publications, 1–80% ratios and messaging findings all match; "strongest predictor" and a consumer-angle claim about people who reject substitutes go beyond the abstract.

studies.title: Researchers build a 12-item test for whether your product gives people something to talk about
studies.paper_title: Product social currency: Conceptualization, measurement and nomological validity
studies.the_study: Across qualitative grounded-theory work and quantitative validation with diverse samples totaling N=2,672, researchers defined and measured "product social currency" — the extent to which a product's attributes and consumption experience provide conversational value and let people express themselves socially. The resulting 12-item scale predicted brand engagement, purchase intention, satisfaction and word of mouth, and was statistically distinct from brand-level social currency.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives product and marketing teams a diagnostic they can run pre-launch on the specific product rather than the brand, separating "people like this" from "people will tell others about this."
studies.story_angle_primary: Consider adding the scale to concept-testing batteries and comparing scores across a portfolio; the brand-versus-product distinction matters most for companies whose strong brand masks individually unremarkable SKUs.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Limited direct relevance for shoppers, beyond the reminder that a lot of product design is explicitly engineered to give buyers a story to tell about themselves.
studies.caveats: Scale-development work relying on self-reported survey measures and stated purchase intention rather than observed purchases or actual word of mouth; predictive validity is cross-sectional and cannot establish causation.
studies.verdict_notes: Construct definition, mixed-methods design, N=2,672, the 12-item scale and its predictive outcomes all align with the abstract.

studies.title: Why the same live-shopping pitch lands differently on Amazon than on Facebook
studies.paper_title: Platform differences in live-streaming commerce: The Role of task-technology fit and social-technology fit in driving consumer engagement and purchase decisions
studies.the_study: Researchers examined how consumers' pre-existing beliefs about a platform shape their response to live-streaming commerce, measuring two kinds of "fit" before participants ever saw a livestream: task-technology fit (is this a good place to shop?) and social-technology fit (is this a good place to interact with people?). Participants assigned to evaluate Amazon rated it high on shopping fit but low on social fit, while Facebook and YouTube showed the reverse pattern. Both types of fit fed engagement and, through engagement, purchase intention — but because Amazon's advantage on one dimension was offset by its deficit on the other, the total indirect effects washed out. Multi-group tests showed the underlying psychological mechanism was the same on every platform; only the starting levels of belief differed.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests live commerce is not a single format that can be replicated across channels: the same broadcast has to compensate for whichever kind of "fit" the host platform lacks, adding social warmth on a retail site or shopping credibility on a social one.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands running livestreams on multiple platforms could test platform-specific formats rather than one master stream — heavier host-audience interaction and community cues on marketplace-style platforms, stronger product demonstration, pricing and purchase-path cues on social video. The study shows this is plausible in a measured sample, not that it lifts sales at scale, so treat it as a hypothesis for a channel-level A/B test.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers arrive at a livestream with expectations already formed by the logo at the top of the screen — the same host selling the same product feels like a sales pitch in one place and a hangout in another, which is worth noticing before you buy on impulse.
studies.caveats: Survey-based study with stimulus exposure and self-reported purchase intention rather than observed purchases; no sample size reported in the abstract; three specific platforms only; the headline mediation effects were partially offsetting and total indirect effects were nonsignificant.
studies.verdict_notes: Fit measures, platform differences, invariance and the nonsignificant total indirect effects are reported correctly; some relative comparisons and associations are tightened into absolute or causal language.

studies.title: Blind boxes inspire two kinds of shoppers — and one of them can't stop
studies.paper_title: From inspired-by to inspired-to: uncovering the factors that influence blind box purchase intention
studies.the_study: A survey of 573 blind box buyers in China tested how the "inspiration" that surprise-packaging retail creates converts into buying, using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Feeling inspired by blind boxes predicted purchase intention through two distinct routes: harmonious passion (a controlled, enjoyable enthusiasm) and obsessive passion (a compulsive pull). Sensation-seeking consumers showed a stronger link between inspiration and obsessive passion, amplifying the problematic pathway.
studies.why_it_matters: Surprise-and-mystery retail formats — blind boxes, loot crates, mystery drops — are among the fastest-growing merchandising tactics, and this evidence says the same design that delights most customers reliably tips a thrill-seeking subset toward compulsive buying.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands building mystery-box or drop-based assortments could examine whether their most profitable repeat buyers are the harmonious kind or the obsessive kind, and test guardrails — purchase caps, pity mechanics, transparent odds, cooling-off prompts — before regulators or media frame the category as gambling-adjacent. This is correlational evidence from one market, so it argues for internal data audits rather than an immediate redesign.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The thrill of not knowing what's in the box is the product, and for people who chase novelty that thrill can shade from fun collecting into chasing — a useful self-check for anyone with a shelf of duplicate figurines.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey of self-selected blind box buyers in a single country (China), so causation cannot be established; outcome is stated purchase intention, not observed spending; all constructs self-reported in one questionnaire.
studies.verdict_notes: Design and mediation/moderation findings are reported correctly, but "Why it matters" asserts a causal, reliable slide into compulsive buying that the cross-sectional intention study cannot support and that contradicts the digest's own caveat.

studies.title: eBay proved its own star ratings were hiding bad sellers — then rewired search to fix it
studies.paper_title: The limits of reputation in platform markets: An empirical analysis and field experiment
studies.the_study: Researchers used transaction-level eBay data to build a seller quality measure based on the share of all transactions that generate positive feedback, including the many transactions where buyers say nothing at all. That measure predicted bad transaction outcomes and buyers' later purchasing even after controlling for the reputation scores shown publicly on the site. eBay then ran a field experiment inserting the hidden quality measure into its search-ranking algorithm: buyers were steered toward higher-quality sellers, subsequent purchasing rose, and conversion on the spot did not fall.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows that visible star ratings are systematically too coarse and too flattering to separate good sellers from bad, and that a marketplace can raise long-run buyer activity simply by reranking search on a better internal quality signal — without paying for it in short-term conversion.
studies.story_angle_primary: Marketplace and retail media teams should ask what their ranking algorithm is actually optimizing: this experiment suggests silence from buyers is information, and that ranking on inferred quality rather than displayed ratings can lift repeat purchasing. It also flags reputational externalities — one bad seller damages trust in the whole platform, which is a case for policing quality even when it costs individual sellers volume.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For shoppers, the lesson is that a seller's public feedback score is a weak guide, partly because disappointed buyers often just walk away without leaving a review. The absence of reviews on a listing may say more than the stars that are there.
studies.caveats: Single platform (eBay) and the field experiment was run by the platform itself, so results reflect eBay's specific search architecture and buyer base; the paper does not establish how long the purchasing gains persist.
studies.verdict_notes: Data, quality measure and field-experiment results match the abstract; "too flattering" and "long-run" go a step beyond what is reported, and the latter sits awkwardly with the digest's own caveat.

studies.title: In livestream selling, more charisma is not better — smiles, looks and volume all peak in the middle
studies.paper_title: Verbal and nonverbal cues in influencer performance: a deep learning perspective on livestreaming e-commerce
studies.the_study: Researchers applied computer vision and audio analysis to 2,346 livestreaming e-commerce videos, extracting nonverbal cues (facial attractiveness, smiling, voice loudness) automatically while manually coding the density of verbal product information, then linked all of it to actual sales. Verbal product information had a straightforwardly positive, linear effect on sales. The nonverbal cues followed inverted-U curves: moderate expressiveness sold best, and both restraint and overdoing it hurt. Crucially, rich verbal content amplified the curve in both directions — good scripts made nonverbal miscalibration more costly, not less.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives livestream retailers an objective, scalable way to audit host performance and suggests that the industry instinct to cast for maximum energy and beauty is wrong past a point.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands running livestream or shoppable video should test host briefs that pair dense product information with deliberately moderated delivery, and consider scoring past streams on these measurable cues rather than relying on gut feel about who is 'good on camera.' The interaction finding is the sharp one: investing in better scripts raises the stakes on host calibration.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Viewers can see why the hyper-enthusiastic, shouty livestream host often fails to convert — audiences appear to read excessive expressiveness as a sales tactic, while steady, informative delivery does the persuading.
studies.caveats: Observational analysis of livestream videos rather than an experiment, so cue effects are correlational; verbal cues were hand-coded while nonverbal cues were machine-extracted; the sample comes from a single livestreaming context and results may not transfer across platforms or product categories.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample size, multimodal method, linear verbal effect, inverted-U nonverbal effects and the amplifying interaction all match; one consumer-facing sentence supplies a mechanism the abstract does not test.

studies.title: Recommendations feel less manipulative when they come from several AIs instead of one
studies.paper_title: Breaking the Single Voice: Perceived AI Plurality as an Autonomy-Supportive Architecture for Ethical Marketplace Decisions
studies.the_study: Three experiments tested what happens when ethical product recommendations are presented as coming from multiple distinct AI agents using different evaluative criteria, rather than from a single algorithmic voice. Perceived plurality raised consumers' self-brand connection; Study 2 showed the mechanism was a heightened sense of autonomy, which in turn lifted purchase intentions. Study 3 found the effect was strongest among consumers with low product knowledge.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the architecture of a recommendation interface — how many voices appear to be advising you — can matter as much as what is recommended, and that plural framing may particularly help less-informed shoppers feel in control.
studies.story_angle_primary: Retailers deploying AI shopping assistants could test multi-agent or multi-criteria presentation (for example, separate 'sustainability,' 'value' and 'durability' advisors) against a single recommendation engine, and watch whether the autonomy gain shows up in real conversion and returns, not just stated intent. It is also a reputational hedge as scrutiny of algorithmic nudging grows.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A practical insight for shoppers: feeling like you chose is easily engineered. If an interface presents several AI 'opinions,' that design may be increasing your comfort with the purchase more than improving the advice.
studies.caveats: Online experiments with hypothetical recommendation scenarios and purchase intentions rather than real purchases; sample details and country not specified in the abstract; no evidence yet that plural framing survives repeated exposure or that the recommendations themselves are better.
studies.verdict_notes: The three-study structure, plurality effect on self–brand connection, autonomy mechanism and low-knowledge moderation are all reported correctly; the headline framing and the "online" descriptor are additions.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- *Displayed trust signals are weaker than structural ones.* The eBay study showing public star ratings systematically fail to separate good sellers from bad, and that reranking on an inferred quality measure lifted subsequent purchasing (Work ID W3121242579), lands on the same conclusion as the previous digest's finding that a platform's authorized-brand badge insulated ad returns while ordinary marketplace listings bled effectiveness as bad reviews accumulated (W7204166660). Both say the credibility doing the work sits in platform architecture, not in the visible score.
- *Sincerity, not disclosure, converts.* "Chinese shoppers reward ESG only when they believe you mean it" (W7214549693) extends the previous digest's suspicion thread — the retailer health endorsement that lowered perceived healthiness (W7203930195) and the "sustainable" label's hidden durability inference (W7208768688). Motive attribution is again the mediator.
- *Persuasion knowledge as the brake.* "Recommendations feel less manipulative when they come from several AIs instead of one" (W7202143753) works through the same consumer defensiveness that previously suppressed spend under vague "up to £100 off" threshold deals (W7203672036).
- *Relationships as a commercial liability.* "When buyers and sellers get too friendly, the platform loses the transaction" (W7214190181) rhymes with the previous finding that relationship and loyalty framing paradoxically licensed customer opportunism (W7172339845): closeness with the customer is not automatically an asset to the firm that brokered it.

**Advances**
- *From funnel mapping to field measurement in video commerce.* The previous digest's AR/VR meta-analysis mapped immersion and vividness onto journey stages using largely lab evidence (W7203672599). This batch pushes the same question into live commerce with harder data: computer vision and audio analysis across 2,346 livestreams linked to actual sales (W7172490860), plus platform-belief effects (W7214279733) and host-type–by–product-type interactions (W7213554170).
- *Reputation research moves from observation to platform-run experiment.* Where W7204166660 was a fixed-effects panel from one seller, W3121242579 pairs a new quality measure with an actual eBay search-ranking field experiment — a meaningful step up in causal strength on the same question.
- *Physical touchpoints as retention machinery.* The previous digest showed that how a customer migrates online predicts lifetime profitability (W7202042423); the new pickup-locker study (W7214672185) identifies the mechanism running the other direction — physical infrastructure reducing churn among existing shoppers rather than acquiring new ones.

**Counterpoints**
- *Merchandising interventions are not reliably positive.* The previous digest's merchandising thread was upbeat: mixed-body mannequins raised willingness to pay (W7203777252), AI-redesigned packs won a real-shelf take-home test (W7207745459). "The 'imported goods' endcap that made imported goods sell 30% worse" (W7213671071) is the hard counterexample — a supplier-funded display format that destroyed nearly a third of unit sales by stripping out the comparison context.
- *Helping shoppers decide can cost you the sale.* The previous digest argued for clarifying trust cues and redirecting shoppers to their own needs to close the advice-taking gap (W7212164165). "Not knowing what you want can make you more likely to buy" (W7213439880) cuts against the reflex: in categories with high inherent outcome variability, preference-clarifying tools may close off the optimism that drives purchase.

**New themes**
- Compulsive-consumption design risk in surprise retail (W7212380221) — not present in the previous batch.
- Cultural localization of AI service agents as a brand-positioning lever (W7214665435), distinct from the previous digest's labeling and packaging work.
- Post-pandemic hygiene cues as a crowding buffer (W7213558307), sentimental-object use raising attachment (W7214807616), hybrid meat acceptance (W7214004504), platform-structured creative labor (W7213556593), and a new product-level social currency scale (W7214728277).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Three studies in this batch, using very different methods, all conclude that live shopping is not one transferable format and that the industry's casting and production instincts are miscalibrated. Computer-vision analysis of 2,346 streams linked to real sales found smiles, attractiveness and vocal volume all follow inverted-U curves, with dense product information the only reliably linear driver ("In livestream selling, more charisma is not better," W7172490860); host type should follow product type, with avatars winning on hedonic goods and humans on utilitarian ones ("Virtual streamers sell fun; human streamers sell function," W7213554170); and the same broadcast lands differently depending on whether the host platform already reads as a shopping place or a social place ("Why the same live-shopping pitch lands differently on Amazon than on Facebook," W7214279733).

**Why pitch this now:** Live and shoppable video is being scaled hard in Western markets just as cheap AI avatar hosts become viable, so brands are making casting, format and platform-portability decisions right now on the assumption that the Chinese playbook copies over intact.

**Angle:** A reported feature on live commerce's transplant problem — what actually moves product on camera versus what the industry keeps buying — built for brand, retail and commerce-media decision-makers, with a consumer-facing thread on why the shouty host is losing to the boring one.

**Potential headlines:**
- What 2,346 livestreams show about who actually sells
- The most charismatic host in live shopping is the wrong one
- Brands are scaling a live commerce format that doesn't travel

**Potential outlets:**
- **Modern Retail** — tracks live and shoppable video rollouts at retailers and DTC brands week to week; this gives the operational counter-evidence its readers are missing.
- **Marketing Brew** — its audience is actively evaluating AI avatar hosts versus creators, and the host-type-by-product-type finding is a concrete decision rule.
- **Adweek** — the casting and talent economics angle (energy and looks past a point hurt sales) sits squarely in its creator and commerce coverage.
- **Rest of World** — the evidence base is largely Chinese and Asian-platform, and the story is precisely about whether a format exports; that transplant question is its core beat.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Pickup lockers don't cannibalize home delivery — they keep customers from leaving (Work ID W7214672185):** Click-and-collect as a churn-reduction tool rather than a logistics saving, with the warning that siting a locker near a strong physical rival hands over your traffic, for a retail trade analysis or e-commerce operations column.
- **Putting EV chargers in the parking lot lifted German grocery revenue 3.4% (Work ID W7213254140):** A hard revenue number on a sustainability amenity, with the twist that the lift comes from stealing competitors' trips in apartment-heavy neighborhoods, for a retail trade explainer or a business-desk piece on the retail side of EV infrastructure.
- **Not knowing what you want can make you more likely to buy (Work ID W7213439880):** Preference quizzes and profiling tools may be killing conversion in wine, fragrance and travel by eliminating the optimism of fuzzy preferences, for a consumer-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet or a CX/personalization trade column.
- **Stop storing your keepsakes — using them makes them mean more (Work ID W7214807616):** The wedding china in the cupboard is losing meaning, not accruing it — a service-y behavioral story with a gifting and jewelry marketing implication, for a general-interest lifestyle or consumer-psychology section.
- **Virtual streamers sell fun; human streamers sell function (Work ID W7213554170):** Match the AI avatar to the product category, not to the budget line — avatars appear to underperform on practical, high-consideration items, for a marketing-trade news brief on AI hosts.
- **The "imported goods" endcap that made imported goods sell 30% worse (Work ID W7213671071):** Supplier-funded display space treated as automatic uplift destroyed a third of sales in a matched-store field test, for a retail/CPG trade explainer on trade-spend assumptions.
- **When buyers and sellers get too friendly, the platform loses the transaction (Work ID W7214190181):** Marketplaces' "successful match" metric may be a churn predictor, and the fix is pricing that survives disintermediation, for a platform-economics column or a business/tech analysis section.
- **Chatbots that get local culture make a foreign retailer feel like a hometown brand (Work ID W7214665435):** Cultural register in the chat window shifted perceived brand localness even among ethnocentric shoppers — a localization story for international e-commerce and CX teams, for a marketing-trade or global-business column.
- **Chinese shoppers reward ESG only when they believe you mean it (Work ID W7214549693):** Sincere-motive framing, not disclosure volume, activated the identification pathway carrying most of the effect, for a sustainability-communications trade piece or a CMO-audience column.
- **Hand sanitizer stations still earn their keep (Work ID W7213558307):** Retailers quietly removed pandemic-era hygiene cues that still buffer the satisfaction penalty of crowded stores, for a retail operations trade brief or a consumer-behavior piece on lingering pandemic habits.
- **The borderless freelance marketplace isn't (Work ID W7213556593):** Four platform-designed frictions degrade the creative work brands are buying offshore — pitchable both as a procurement warning and as a labor story, for an agency/brand-strategy column or a general-interest gig-economy feature.
- **Blended burgers keep surprising people (Work ID W7214004504):** Seventy-nine studies suggest the ceiling on replacing meat in hybrids is far higher than product teams assume, and taste beats concept, for a food-industry trade explainer or a food-and-climate section in a general-interest outlet.
- **Researchers build a 12-item test for whether your product gives people something to talk about (Work ID W7214728277):** A pre-launch diagnostic separating "people like this" from "people will tell others," useful for companies whose strong brand masks unremarkable SKUs, for a product-marketing or insights trade brief.
- **Why the same live-shopping pitch lands differently on Amazon than on Facebook (Work ID W7214279733):** Shoppers arrive with platform beliefs already formed, so a single master livestream has to compensate for whichever kind of fit the host platform lacks, for a commerce-media trade analysis.
- **Blind boxes inspire two kinds of shoppers — and one of them can't stop (Work ID W7212380221):** Sensation-seeking buyers convert inspiration into compulsive passion, raising the gambling-adjacent regulatory question before regulators ask it, for a consumer-affairs piece or a retail-trade story on mystery-box merchandising guardrails.
- **eBay proved its own star ratings were hiding bad sellers — then rewired search to fix it (Work ID W3121242579):** Buyer silence is information, and reranking on inferred quality raised repeat purchasing without costing conversion — a rare platform-run field experiment, for a marketplace/retail-media trade analysis, with a consumer sidebar on why review scores mislead.
- **In livestream selling, more charisma is not better (Work ID W7172490860):** Inverted-U curves on smiling, looks and volume, and better scripts make miscalibrated delivery more costly, not less, for a creator-economy or commerce-video trade piece.
- **Recommendations feel less manipulative when they come from several AIs instead of one (Work ID W7202143753):** Splitting an AI shopping assistant into multiple criteria-specific advisors raised felt autonomy and purchase intent, especially among low-knowledge shoppers — engineered choice, for an AI-in-retail trade column or a consumer-tech explainer on algorithmic nudging.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Retail & E-Commerce — 2026-09-30 (Part 2)
**Checked:** 2026-09-30 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: Pickup lockers don't cannibalize home delivery — they keep customers from leaving
**Work ID:** W7214672185 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Dropped moderators** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and the benefit shrank when stations were placed close to major offline retail alternatives"
- **Abstract says:** "these positive effects are moderated by: station accessibility, level of nearby offline competition, and product attributes"
- **Problem:** The digest reports only the offline-competition moderator; station accessibility and product attributes (which the abstract ties to "product suitability" implications for managers) are omitted, so readers get a narrower boundary condition than the paper states.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add a clause noting the effect also depended on station accessibility and on product attributes, per the abstract."

### Study 2: Putting EV chargers in the parking lot lifted German grocery revenue 3.4%
**Work ID:** W7213254140 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unstated direction of moderators** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the data suggest rollout should be prioritized where parking is ample, competition is close, and shoppers live in apartments without home charging"
- **Abstract says:** "provide insights into the role of various store (surface-to-parking ratio, management type) and market (e.g., local competition, apartment-to-house ratio, neighborhood wealth) characteristics"
- **Problem:** The abstract names these characteristics but does not report the direction of their moderating effects, so the specific prioritization advice (ample parking, close competition, apartment-dwellers) is not verifiable from the abstract and reads as an established result.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the paper identifies these store and market characteristics as conditions that shape the effect, without asserting which direction each runs, or mark the prioritization as an inference to be checked in the full paper."

**Issue B. Moderator wording** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Effects were stronger in stores and neighborhoods with particular characteristics, including surface-to-parking ratio, local competition, and the mix of apartments versus houses."
- **Abstract says:** "They identify several attitudinal (perceived impulsiveness, storability) and behavioral (penetration, purchase frequency) category characteristics that explain where the revenue increase comes from and provide insights into the role of various store ... and market ... characteristics."
- **Problem:** "Effects were stronger in stores and neighborhoods with particular characteristics" implies a tested stronger/weaker split; the abstract only says the authors provide insight into the role of these characteristics.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase to "the paper examines how store and market characteristics — surface-to-parking ratio, local competition, apartment-to-house ratio — relate to the size of the effect.""

### Study 3: Not knowing what you want can make you more likely to buy
**Work ID:** W7213439880 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 4: Stop storing your keepsakes — using them makes them mean more
**Work ID:** W7214807616 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Design detail not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Laboratory and online experiments rather than long-run field observation"
- **Abstract says:** "Across five studies, we show that usage of sentimentally valuable objects increases their sentimental value."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not describe the studies as laboratory or online experiments, nor does it give time horizons. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "State that the abstract does not specify study formats or time horizons, rather than characterizing them as lab and online experiments."

### Study 5: Virtual streamers sell fun; human streamers sell function
**Work ID:** W7213554170 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: The "imported goods" endcap that made imported goods sell 30% worse
**Work ID:** W7213671071 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Field-test window** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Researchers ran a 60-day field test with a local supermarket chain in Turkiye"
- **Abstract says:** "their sales performance was tracked for 60 days before and after the intervention, with a matched control store for comparison"
- **Problem:** Sales were tracked for 60 days before and 60 days after the intervention, not a single 60-day test period.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "tracked sales for 60 days before and 60 days after the change.""

### Study 7: When buyers and sellers get too friendly, the platform loses the transaction
**Work ID:** W7214190181 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 8: Chatbots that get local culture make a foreign retailer feel like a hometown brand
**Work ID:** W7214665435 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 9: Chinese shoppers reward ESG only when they believe you mean it
**Work ID:** W7214549693 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mediation share overstated** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the mediating variable that carried most of the effect here"
- **Abstract says:** "with the indirect effect through identification accounting for 38.3% of the total effect, revealing a "dual-channel structure" in which a direct effect and an indirect, identification-mediated effect coexist"
- **Problem:** 38.3% is a minority of the total effect; the abstract explicitly describes a dual-channel structure in which the direct effect coexists. Saying identification "carried most of the effect" reverses the relative weighting.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "the mediating variable that carried about 38% of the total effect, alongside a direct effect.""

**Issue B. Skeptical consumers vs. skeptical environments** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "ESG performance raised purchase intention even among skeptical consumers"
- **Abstract says:** "corporate ESG performance exerts a robust positive effect on purchase intention even in skeptical environments"
- **Problem:** The abstract refers to skeptical environments (a market backdrop of greenwashing skepticism), not to a measured segment of skeptical consumers.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "even against a backdrop of widespread greenwashing skepticism.""

### Study 10: Hand sanitizer stations still earn their keep: visible hygiene cues soften shoppers' dislike of crowded stores
**Work ID:** W7213558307 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Density vs. perceived crowding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "crowding lowered shopping satisfaction, but that penalty shrank when visible hygiene cues were present"
- **Abstract says:** "Results showed that higher density reduced satisfaction, but this negative effect was attenuated when sanitary signals were present. Perceived crowding did not mediate the density–satisfaction relationship."
- **Problem:** The satisfaction effect came from manipulated store density; the abstract specifically reports that perceived crowding did not mediate it. Using "crowding" and dropping the null mediation blurs a finding the authors flag.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "higher store density lowered satisfaction — though perceived crowding did not explain the link — and the penalty shrank when hygiene cues were present.""

**Issue B. Country claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Single country (French-language sample)"
- **Abstract says:** "A two-study design was implemented within a single French-language survey (N = 425)."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives the survey language, not a country; a French-language sample could span several countries. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Describe it as "a single French-language survey pool (country not specified in the abstract).""

### Study 11: The borderless freelance marketplace isn't: four frictions that quietly kill creative work on global platforms
**Work ID:** W7213556593 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline overstates effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "four frictions that quietly kill creative work on global platforms"
- **Abstract says:** "four dualistic tensions, organizing, performing, belonging, and learning , that systematically constrain the creative processes of freelancers"
- **Problem:** "Kill" implies creative work is destroyed; the abstract reports tensions that constrain creative processes, with no measure of output loss.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "constrain" or "hold back" instead of "kill"."

**Issue B. Unverifiable mechanism detail** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "since platform metrics that reward speed and compliance can suppress the creative risk-taking you are paying for"
- **Abstract says:** "platform mechanisms shape creative realization in cross-border freelancer–client relationships, particularly under culturally heterogeneous service norms and Global North–South economic asymmetries"
- **Problem:** The specific claim about speed- and compliance-rewarding metrics is not stated in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute the specific metric claim to the full paper or soften to "platform mechanisms" as the abstract phrases it. Unverifiable from abstract only."

### Study 12: Blended burgers keep surprising people: review of 79 studies finds hybrid meat wins on taste more often than expected
**Work ID:** W7214004504 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Strongest predictor" overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "sensory appeal was the strongest predictor of liking"
- **Abstract says:** "Sensory appeal emerged as a strong predictor of liking and acceptance"
- **Problem:** The abstract says "a strong predictor," not that it ranked as the strongest among predictors.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "sensory appeal emerged as a strong predictor of liking"."

**Issue B. Unsupported subgroup claim** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Consumers who reject meat substitutes outright often like hybrid products when they actually taste them"
- **Abstract says:** "Across studies, hybrid meat products generally showed high consumer acceptance, liking, and preference, often exceeding expectations."
- **Problem:** The abstract makes no claim about consumers who reject plant-based substitutes; this invents a subgroup finding the review does not report in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase to "Acceptance of hybrid products was generally high and often exceeded people's expectations" without the rejecter subgroup."

**Issue C. Extrapolated replacement ceiling** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the evidence suggests the ceiling on how much meat you can replace is higher than most product teams assume"
- **Abstract says:** "a wide range of ingredients and non-meat ratios (1% to 80%) were generally well accepted"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the range studied was well accepted; it says nothing about industry assumptions or a ceiling.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "non-meat ratios as high as 80% were generally well accepted in the studies reviewed"."

### Study 13: Researchers build a 12-item test for whether your product gives people something to talk about
**Work ID:** W7214728277 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 14: Why the same live-shopping pitch lands differently on Amazon than on Facebook
**Work ID:** W7214279733 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Relative comparison stated as absolute levels** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Participants assigned to evaluate Amazon rated it high on shopping fit but low on social fit, while Facebook and YouTube showed the reverse pattern."
- **Abstract says:** "Participants evaluating Amazon reported higher TTF and lower STF than those evaluating Facebook or YouTube."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports only a relative difference between platforms, not that Amazon scored absolutely "high"/"low" or that the other platforms mirrored the pattern.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "rated Amazon higher on shopping fit and lower on social fit than Facebook or YouTube"."

**Issue B. Causal verb for associational paths** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Both types of fit fed engagement and, through engagement, purchase intention"
- **Abstract says:** "Both forms of fit were positively associated with consumer engagement and, through engagement, with purchase intention."
- **Problem:** "Fed" implies a causal flow; the abstract describes positive associations in a survey-based model.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "were positively associated with engagement and, through engagement, with purchase intention"."

**Issue C. Added interpretation of offsetting effects** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "but because Amazon's advantage on one dimension was offset by its deficit on the other, the total indirect effects washed out"
- **Abstract says:** "The two focal serial indirect effects ran in opposite directions and partially offset one another, while the total indirect effects were nonsignificant."
- **Problem:** The abstract states the two indirect effects ran in opposite directions and partially offset; the Amazon-specific explanation is the digest's own reading.
- **Suggested fix:** "State that the two indirect effects ran in opposite directions and partially cancelled, leaving total indirect effects nonsignificant."

### Study 15: Blind boxes inspire two kinds of shoppers — and one of them can't stop
**Work ID:** W7212380221 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Causal and outcome overstatement** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "this evidence says the same design that delights most customers reliably tips a thrill-seeking subset toward compulsive buying"
- **Abstract says:** "an inspired-by state positively influences customers' purchase intention, with HP and OP mediating this relationship. Sensation-seeking positively moderates the relationship between the inspired-by state and OP"
- **Problem:** The study is a cross-sectional survey measuring obsessive passion and purchase intention, not compulsive buying behavior; "reliably tips" asserts causation the design cannot support and contradicts the digest's own caveat that causation cannot be established.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rewrite as "sensation-seeking buyers showed a stronger link between inspiration and obsessive passion, a pathway the authors associate with excessive purchasing"."

**Issue B. Unsupported market-growth claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Surprise-and-mystery retail formats — blind boxes, loot crates, mystery drops — are among the fastest-growing merchandising tactics"
- **Abstract says:** "Blind box retailing is becoming a prominent marketing strategy."
- **Problem:** The abstract only calls the format prominent and growing in popularity; the ranking claim about fastest-growing tactics is not supported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "blind box retailing is a fast-growing format, per the authors"."

### Study 16: eBay proved its own star ratings were hiding bad sellers — then rewired search to fix it
**Work ID:** W3121242579 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Direction of bias specified** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "visible star ratings are systematically too coarse and too flattering to separate good sellers from bad"
- **Abstract says:** "public reputation measures may be biased or too coarse to let buyers accurately infer seller quality"
- **Problem:** The abstract says public measures may be biased or too coarse without specifying that the bias is upward/flattering.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop "too flattering" or say "biased and too coarse"."

**Issue B. "Long-run" gains overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a marketplace can raise long-run buyer activity simply by reranking search on a better internal quality signal"
- **Abstract says:** "The treatment shifted buyers toward higher-quality sellers and increased subsequent purchasing without reducing contemporaneous conversion."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports increased subsequent purchasing, not long-run activity; the body text also conflicts with the digest's caveat that persistence is not established.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change "long-run buyer activity" to "subsequent purchasing"."

**Issue C. Embellished frequency of silent transactions** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "including the many transactions where buyers say nothing at all"
- **Abstract says:** "including transactions for which buyers leave no feedback"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not quantify how common no-feedback transactions are.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "including transactions where buyers leave no feedback"."

### Study 17: In livestream selling, more charisma is not better — smiles, looks and volume all peak in the middle
**Work ID:** W7172490860 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported mechanism for the inverted U** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "audiences appear to read excessive expressiveness as a sales tactic, while steady, informative delivery does the persuading"
- **Abstract says:** "nonverbal cues exhibit inverted U-shaped relationships − moderate levels are most effective, with both under- and over-expression reducing sales"
- **Problem:** The abstract documents the shape of the effect but does not test or report viewer inferences about sales tactics.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that over-expression reduced sales without asserting why, or label the interpretation as speculation."

### Study 18: Recommendations feel less manipulative when they come from several AIs instead of one
**Work ID:** W7202143753 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline outcome not measured** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Recommendations feel less manipulative when they come from several AIs instead of one"
- **Abstract says:** "structuring ethical recommendations through a plural AI architecture enhances consumers' self–brand connection. Study 2 demonstrates that plural recommendations increase perceived autonomy"
- **Problem:** Perceived manipulativeness was not among the measured outcomes named in the abstract; the measured constructs were autonomy, self–brand connection and purchase intention.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe headline around feeling more in control/autonomous rather than less manipulated."

**Issue B. Study mode assumed** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Online experiments with hypothetical recommendation scenarios and purchase intentions rather than real purchases"
- **Abstract says:** "Across three experiments, this research examines the societal and psychological implications of perceived algorithmic plurality"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state that the experiments were run online or that scenarios were hypothetical.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "three experiments measuring stated purchase intentions rather than real purchases; delivery mode not specified in the abstract." Unverifiable from abstract only."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Pickup lockers don't cannibalize home delivery — they keep customers from leaving | ⚠️ Minor issues | Core findings match the abstract; two of the three named moderators (station accessibility, product attributes) are dropped. |
| 2 | Putting EV chargers in the parking lot lifted German grocery revenue 3.4% | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, sample and the 3.4% effect are reported accurately; the story angle assigns directions to store/market moderators that the abstract does not state. |
| 3 | Not knowing what you want can make you more likely to buy | ✅ Accurate | Uncertainty types, direction of effect, optimism mechanism and the purchase-intent outcome all match; caveats correctly note unspecified samples. |
| 4 | Stop storing your keepsakes — using them makes them mean more | ⚠️ Minor issues | Five studies, direction of effect and the salience/self-concept mechanism match; the caveat asserts a study format the abstract never states. |
| 5 | Virtual streamers sell fun; human streamers sell function | ✅ Accurate | Two scenario-based experiments, the streamer-by-product interaction, social-presence mediation and brand-trust moderation are all reported as in the abstract; "high-consideration" in the story angle is an added descriptor but is framed as a hypothesis to test. |
| 6 | The "imported goods" endcap that made imported goods sell 30% worse | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sales decline, survey Ns, country comparison and variance explained all match; the field test window is described slightly inaccurately. |
| 7 | When buyers and sellers get too friendly, the platform loses the transaction | ✅ Accurate | Data source, two-way fixed effects, direction of the carrier associations, the shipper non-robustness and the paper's own hedged interpretation are all represented correctly. |
| 8 | Chatbots that get local culture make a foreign retailer feel like a hometown brand | ✅ Accurate | Mixed-methods design (15 interviews, 303 online-recruited consumers, SEM), the localness–identification–co-creation chain, the null ethnocentrism moderation and the single-retailer/single-market boundary all match the abstract. |
| 9 | Chinese shoppers reward ESG only when they believe you mean it | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study designs, Ns and the 38.3% indirect effect are correct, but one story-angle line overstates the identification channel as carrying most of the effect. |
| 10 | Hand sanitizer stations still earn their keep: visible hygiene cues soften shoppers' dislike of crowded stores | ⚠️ Minor issues | N, two-study structure inside one survey, and the density-by-sanitary-signal result are right; the digest conflates manipulated density with perceived crowding and omits the null mediation, and it asserts a single country not stated in the abstract. |
| 11 | The borderless freelance marketplace isn't: four frictions that quietly kill creative work on global platforms | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, samples and the four tensions match the abstract; headline verb and one story-angle specific go slightly beyond it. |
